name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Hybridisation and geometry change in boron trichloride ammonia adduct

questiontext.text:
Observe the structural transformation shown in the diagram below for the reaction of \(\mathrm{BCl_3}\) with \(\mathrm{NH_3}\):

What is the change in hybridisation of the boron atom and the geometry around it during this reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows planar \(\mathrm{BCl_3}\) reacting with \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) to form the tetrahedral adduct \(\mathrm{BCl_3\cdot NH_3}\), in which boron is bonded to three chlorine atoms and one nitrogen atom of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In covalent molecules and Lewis acid-base adducts, the hybridisation of the central atom is determined by the total number of \(\sigma\)-bond pairs plus lone pairs around it (steric number).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Steric number} = \text{Number of }\sigma\text{-bonds} + \text{Number of lone pairs on central atom}\). A steric number of \(3\) corresponds to \(sp^2\) hybridisation (trigonal planar), and a steric number of \(4\) corresponds to \(sp^3\) hybridisation (tetrahedral).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In \(\mathrm{BCl_3}\), boron has \(3\) valence electrons shared with \(3\) chlorine atoms, giving \(3\) \(\sigma\)-bonds and \(0\) lone pairs (steric number \(= 3\)). Thus, boron is \(sp^2\) hybridised with trigonal planar geometry. Upon accepting a lone pair of electrons from \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), boron forms a fourth \(\sigma\) (coordinate) bond to nitrogen. Now boron has \(4\) \(\sigma\)-bonds and \(0\) lone pairs (steric number \(= 4\)), so its hybridisation changes to \(sp^3\) with tetrahedral geometry.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Boron completes its octet (\(8\) electrons) in the adduct without exceeding its maximum covalence of \(4\). Therefore, the hybridisation and geometry of boron change from \(sp^2\) (trigonal planar) to \(sp^3\) (tetrahedral).

answer.text: \(sp^2\) (trigonal planar) to \(sp^3\) (tetrahedral)
\(sp\) (linear) to \(sp^2\) (trigonal planar)
\(sp^3\) (tetrahedral) to \(sp^3d\) (trigonal bipyramidal)
\(sp^2\) (trigonal planar) to \(dsp^2\) (square planar)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Hydrogen bonding in layered structure of orthoboric acid

questiontext.text:
The diagram below represents a portion of the two-dimensional layered structure of orthoboric acid (\(\mathrm{H_3BO_3}\)):

What do the dotted lines connecting adjacent planar \(\mathrm{BO_3}\) units represent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows planar triangular \(\mathrm{BO_3}\) units of orthoboric acid (\(\mathrm{H_3BO_3}\)) arranged in a two-dimensional sheet, with dotted lines connecting \(\mathrm{H}\) atoms of one \(\mathrm{BO_3}\) unit to \(\mathrm{O}\) atoms of an adjacent \(\mathrm{BO_3}\) unit.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Solid lines represent covalent \(\mathrm{B-O}\) and \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bonds within an individual \(\mathrm{B(OH)_3}\) molecule, whereas dotted lines represent intermolecular interactions between neighbouring molecules.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
When a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a strongly electronegative atom like oxygen, it experiences an attractive electrostatic interaction with a lone pair on an oxygen atom of a neighbouring molecule, forming an intermolecular hydrogen bond (\(\mathrm{O-H \cdots O}\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Each \(\mathrm{B(OH)_3}\) unit has three \(\mathrm{-OH}\) groups in a trigonal planar arrangement around boron. The \(\mathrm{H}\) atom of an \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group on one molecule forms a dotted-line \(\mathrm{O-H \cdots O}\) hydrogen bond with an \(\mathrm{O}\) atom of a neighbouring molecule, linking the planar \(\mathrm{BO_3}\) units into a continuous two-dimensional sheet (polymeric layer structure).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
This hydrogen-bonded layered structure accounts for the soapy touch and polymeric nature of crystalline boric acid. Thus, the dotted lines represent intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

answer.text: Coordinate covalent bonds
Three-centre two-electron bonds
Intermolecular hydrogen bonds
London dispersion forces

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Structure and bond parameters of aluminium chloride dimer

questiontext.text:
The dimeric structure of anhydrous aluminium chloride (\(\mathrm{Al_2Cl_6}\)) is shown below with its bond lengths and bond angles:

Which statement accurately describes the bonding and geometry in \(\mathrm{Al_2Cl_6}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows the \(\mathrm{Al_2Cl_6}\) dimer with terminal \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bond length \(= 206\text{ pm}\), bridging \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bond length \(= 221\text{ pm}\), internal bridging \(\angle\mathrm{Cl-Al-Cl} = 79^\circ\), external terminal \(\angle\mathrm{Cl-Al-Cl} = 118^\circ\), and \(\angle\mathrm{Al-Cl-Al} = 101^\circ\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In monomeric \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\), aluminium has only \(6\) valence electrons (electron-deficient). It achieves an octet by dimerising via halogen bridging, where a chlorine atom of one \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) unit donates a lone pair to the aluminium atom of the other unit.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Each \(\mathrm{Al}\) atom in \(\mathrm{Al_2Cl_6}\) forms \(4\) \(\sigma\)-bonds (two terminal \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bonds and two bridging \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bonds) with \(0\) lone pairs, corresponding to \(sp^3\) hybridisation and tetrahedral geometry.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because each \(\mathrm{Al}\) atom is surrounded by four \(\mathrm{Cl}\) atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement, its hybridisation is \(sp^3\). The two terminal \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bonds are normal \(2c\text{-}2e\) covalent bonds with a shorter bond length of \(206\text{ pm}\), whereas the bridging \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bonds involve coordinate donation from \(\mathrm{Cl}\) to \(\mathrm{Al}\) (sharing electron density between two \(\mathrm{Al}\) centres) and are weaker and longer (\(221\text{ pm}\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Consistent with the diagram, each \(\mathrm{Al}\) atom is \(sp^3\) hybridised in a tetrahedral environment, and the bridging \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bonds (\(221\text{ pm}\)) are longer than the terminal \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bonds (\(206\text{ pm}\)).

answer.text: Each \(\mathrm{Al}\) atom is \(sp^2\) hybridised, and bridging \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bonds are shorter than terminal \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bonds.

Each \(\mathrm{Al}\) atom is \(sp^3\) hybridised in a tetrahedral geometry, and bridging \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bonds (\(221\text{ pm}\)) are longer than terminal \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bonds (\(206\text{ pm}\)).
Each \(\mathrm{Al}\) atom uses \(3d\)-orbitals to achieve \(sp^3d^2\) hybridisation by forming six \(\mathrm{Al-Cl}\) bonds.
The bridging \(\mathrm{Al-Cl-Al}\) bonds are three-centre two-electron bonds identical to those in diborane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Planarity and bridge bond electrons in diborane

questiontext.text:
The structure of diborane (\(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\)) with its bond lengths and bond angles is shown below:

From the structural diagram of diborane, how many atoms lie in the same plane, and how many electrons are involved in each bridging \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bond?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram of \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\) shows \(2\) boron atoms, \(4\) terminal hydrogen atoms (with \(\mathrm{B-H}\) bond length \(119\text{ pm}\) and terminal \(\angle\mathrm{H-B-H} = 120^\circ\)), and \(2\) bridging hydrogen atoms (with \(\mathrm{B-H}\) bond length \(134\text{ pm}\) and \(\angle\mathrm{H-B-H} = 97^\circ\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Diborane has \(12\) total valence electrons (\(3 \times 2 = 6\) from two \(\mathrm{B}\) atoms and \(1 \times 6 = 6\) from six \(\mathrm{H}\) atoms).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Terminal \(\mathrm{B-H}\) bonds are regular two-centre two-electron (\(2c\text{-}2e\)) bonds, whereas the two bridging \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bonds are three-centre two-electron (\(3c\text{-}2e\)) bonds.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Planarity: As indicated by the dashed parallelogram in the diagram, the \(4\) terminal hydrogen atoms and the \(2\) boron atoms lie in one plane, giving \(4 + 2 = 6\) coplanar atoms. The \(2\) bridging hydrogen atoms lie above and below this plane.
2. Electron count in bridge bonds: Out of \(12\) valence electrons, the \(4\) terminal \(2c\text{-}2e\) bonds use \(4 \times 2 = 8\) electrons. The remaining \(12 - 8 = 4\) electrons are shared equally between the \(2\) bridging \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bonds, so each \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bridge bond contains \(2\) electrons.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(6\) atoms are coplanar and each bridging \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bond is a \(3c\text{-}2e\) bond involving \(2\) electrons.

answer.text: \(4\) atoms lie in one plane; \(2\) electrons in each \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bond
\(6\) atoms lie in one plane; \(4\) electrons in each \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bond
\(8\) atoms lie in one plane; \(2\) electrons in each \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bond
\(6\) atoms lie in one plane; \(2\) electrons in each \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bond

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_DIAGRAM_Q05 - Orbital overlap in banana bonds of diborane

questiontext.text:
The orbital overlap diagram for bonding in diborane (\(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\)) is shown below (dashed lobes represent empty \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals):

Which combination of atomic/hybrid orbitals overlaps to form one bridging \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) (banana) bond?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The orbital diagram shows each boron atom using four \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals (three half-filled, shown with shaded overlap, and one empty, shown with dashed lines) and six hydrogen \(1s\) orbitals.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In its excited state, boron has the configuration \(1s^2 2s^1 2p_x^1 2p_y^1 2p_z^0\). Upon \(sp^3\) hybridisation, boron forms four \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals, of which three contain one electron each and one is vacant.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
A three-centre two-electron (\(3c\text{-}2e\)) bond is formed by the simultaneous overlap of three orbitals containing a total of two electrons.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Two half-filled \(sp^3\) orbitals on each boron atom overlap with \(1s\) orbitals of two terminal hydrogen atoms to form two normal \(2c\text{-}2e\) bonds. That leaves one half-filled \(sp^3\) orbital and one vacant \(sp^3\) orbital on each boron atom. For each bridging \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bond, one half-filled \(sp^3\) orbital from one \(\mathrm{B}\) atom, one vacant \(sp^3\) orbital from the second \(\mathrm{B}\) atom, and one half-filled \(1s\) orbital of the bridging \(\mathrm{H}\) atom overlap simultaneously, accommodating \(1 + 0 + 1 = 2\) electrons.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Total orbitals overlapping \(= 3\), total electrons \(= 2\), forming the \(3c\text{-}2e\) banana bond. Therefore, one half-filled \(sp^3\) orbital of one \(\mathrm{B}\) atom, one vacant \(sp^3\) orbital of the other \(\mathrm{B}\) atom, and one half-filled \(1s\) orbital of \(\mathrm{H}\) form each bridging bond.

answer.text: One half-filled \(sp^3\) orbital of one \(\mathrm{B}\) atom, one vacant \(sp^3\) orbital of the other \(\mathrm{B}\) atom, and one half-filled \(1s\) orbital of \(\mathrm{H}\)
Two half-filled \(sp^3\) orbitals (one from each \(\mathrm{B}\) atom) and one vacant \(1s\) orbital of \(\mathrm{H}\)
Two vacant \(sp^3\) orbitals (one from each \(\mathrm{B}\) atom) and one half-filled \(1s\) orbital of \(\mathrm{H}\)
One half-filled \(sp^2\) orbital of one \(\mathrm{B}\) atom, one unhybridised \(2p\) orbital of the other \(\mathrm{B}\) atom, and one \(1s\) orbital of \(\mathrm{H}\)

questiontext.text:
The reaction scheme below illustrates the hydrolysis of silicon tetrachloride (\(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\)) to silicic acid:

Why does \(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\) readily undergo the initial nucleophilic attack by water shown in the diagram, whereas \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\) does not?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows the oxygen atom of \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) donating a lone pair of electrons to the central \(\mathrm{Si}\) atom of \(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\), followed by elimination of \(\mathrm{HCl}\) to yield \(\mathrm{SiCl_3(OH)}\) and eventually \(\mathrm{Si(OH)_4}\) (silicic acid).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In \(\mathrm{MCl_4}\) molecules of Group \(14\), the central atom already has \(8\) valence electrons (four \(\sigma\)-bonds). Accepting an additional lone pair from \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) requires an empty low-energy orbital on the central atom.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Second-period elements (like carbon, \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^2\)) lack \(d\)-orbitals and cannot expand their covalence beyond \(4\), whereas third-period elements (like silicon, \([\mathrm{Ne}]3s^2 3p^2\)) have vacant \(3d\)-orbitals.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
When \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) approaches \(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\), silicon accommodates the lone pair of electrons from the oxygen atom of \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) in its vacant \(3d\)-orbitals, forming a \(5\)-coordinated intermediate that loses \(\mathrm{HCl}\). Repetition of this step replaces all four \(\mathrm{Cl}\) atoms with \(\mathrm{-OH}\) groups to form \(\mathrm{Si(OH)_4}\). In \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\), carbon has no vacant \(d\)-orbitals in its \(n=2\) valence shell, so it cannot accept a lone pair from water.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, \(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\) undergoes hydrolysis readily because silicon has vacant \(3d\)-orbitals to accept a lone pair from water, whereas carbon lacks \(d\)-orbitals.

answer.text: Silicon has a higher electronegativity than carbon, attracting the oxygen atom of water more strongly.
Silicon can accept a lone pair of electrons from the oxygen atom of water into its vacant \(3d\)-orbitals, whereas carbon lacks \(d\)-orbitals.
Silicon forms ionic \(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\) ions in water, whereas \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\) is purely covalent.
Carbon has a larger atomic radius than silicon, causing steric hindrance around the central atom.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_DIAGRAM_Q07 - Atomic radius trend across Group 13 elements

questiontext.text:
The bar chart below displays the atomic radii (in \(\text{pm}\)) of Group \(13\) elements from Boron (\(\mathrm{B}\)) to Thallium (\(\mathrm{Tl}\)):

What is the primary cause of the decrease in atomic radius at Gallium (\(\mathrm{Ga}\)) compared to Aluminium (\(\mathrm{Al}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The bar chart shows the atomic radii of Group \(13\) elements: \(\mathrm{B} = 88\text{ pm}\), \(\mathrm{Al} = 143\text{ pm}\), \(\mathrm{Ga} = 135\text{ pm}\), \(\mathrm{In} = 167\text{ pm}\), and \(\mathrm{Tl} = 170\text{ pm}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
On moving down a group, each successive element adds a new principal shell, which normally increases atomic radius. Deviations occur when the inner-core electronic configuration changes.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Effective nuclear charge \(Z_{\text{eff}} = Z - \sigma\), where \(\sigma\) is the shielding constant. Shielding ability decreases in the order \(s > p > d > f\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Aluminium has a noble-gas inner core (\([\mathrm{Ne}]3s^2 3p^1\)), whereas gallium has an inner core containing \(10\) additional \(3d\)-electrons (\([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10} 4s^2 4p^1\)) and a nuclear charge higher by \(18\) units. Because the \(10\) \(3d\)-electrons offer poor shielding for the outer \(4s\) and \(4p\) electrons, the increased nuclear charge pulls the valence shell inward, reducing the atomic radius of \(\mathrm{Ga}\) (\(135\text{ pm}\)) below that of \(\mathrm{Al}\) (\(143\text{ pm}\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The anomaly at \(\mathrm{Ga}\) (\(135\text{ pm} < 143\text{ pm}\)) is due to the poor shielding effect of the \(10\) inner \(3d\)-electrons in gallium.

answer.text: The presence of \(14\) inner \(4f\)-electrons in gallium
The inert pair effect of the \(4s^2\) electrons in gallium
Poor shielding of outer electrons by the \(10\) inner \(3d\)-electrons in gallium
Higher first ionisation enthalpy of aluminium compared to gallium

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_DIAGRAM_Q08 - Structural comparison of diamond and graphite allotropes

questiontext.text:
The diagrams below compare two crystalline allotropes of carbon: (I) a rigid three-dimensional tetrahedral network and (II) a layered hexagonal sheet structure:

Which statement accurately matches the hybridisation, \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond length, and interlayer bonding of these two allotropes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Structure (I) shows a 3D tetrahedral network (diamond) with a \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond length of \(154\text{ pm}\). Structure (II) shows planar hexagonal layers (graphite) with an in-plane \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond length of \(141.5\text{ pm}\) and an interlayer distance of \(340\text{ pm}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Bond length decreases as \(s\)-character and bond order increase. Interlayer forces between neutral covalent sheets are non-covalent van der Waals interactions.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In diamond, each carbon forms \(4\) \(\sigma\)-bonds (\(sp^3\)). In graphite, each carbon forms \(3\) \(\sigma\)-bonds (\(sp^2\)) and one delocalised \(\pi\)-bond across the hexagonal sheet.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In diamond, every carbon atom is \(sp^3\) hybridised and tetrahedrally bonded to four neighbours with single \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bonds of length \(154\text{ pm}\). In graphite, every carbon atom is \(sp^2\) hybridised, forming three \(\sigma\)-bonds within the hexagonal layer and a delocalised \(\pi\)-system, giving a shorter \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond length of \(141.5\text{ pm}\) (partial double-bond character). Adjacent sheets are separated by \(340\text{ pm}\) and held together by weak van der Waals forces.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, diamond has \(sp^3\) carbons with \(154\text{ pm}\) bonds in a 3D network, whereas graphite has \(sp^2\) carbons with \(141.5\text{ pm}\) in-layer bonds and \(340\text{ pm}\) interlayer spacing held by van der Waals forces.

answer.text: Diamond has \(sp^2\) carbons with \(154\text{ pm}\) bonds; graphite has \(sp^3\) carbons with \(141.5\text{ pm}\) in-layer bonds.
Diamond has \(sp^3\) carbons with \(141.5\text{ pm}\) bonds; graphite has \(sp^2\) carbons with \(154\text{ pm}\) in-layer bonds and covalent interlayer bonds.
Both diamond and graphite have \(sp^3\) carbons, and the \(340\text{ pm}\) interlayer distance in graphite is due to hydrogen bonding.

Diamond has \(sp^3\) carbons with \(154\text{ pm}\) bonds in a 3D network; graphite has \(sp^2\) carbons with \(141.5\text{ pm}\) in-layer bonds and \(340\text{ pm}\) interlayer spacing held by van der Waals forces.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_DIAGRAM_Q09 - Ring composition and fusion in Buckminsterfullerene C60

questiontext.text:
The soccer-ball-shaped cage structure of Buckminsterfullerene (\(\mathrm{C_{60}}\)) is represented below:

How many six-membered and five-membered rings are present in \(\mathrm{C_{60}}\), and what ring-fusion rule applies to this structure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows the cage-like soccer-ball structure of \(\mathrm{C_{60}}\) (Buckminsterfullerene), consisting of \(60\) equivalent \(sp^2\)-hybridised carbon vertices arranged in fused five-membered and six-membered rings.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In \(\mathrm{C_{60}}\), each vertex is shared by three rings, and no two five-membered rings share an edge (isolated pentagon rule).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Euler's polyhedron formula for a closed cage of pentagons (\(P\)) and hexagons (\(H\)) where every vertex has degree \(3\), \(P = 12\) is fixed, and \(5P + 6H = 3V = 3(60) = 180\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting \(P = 12\) into \(5P + 6H = 180\):
\[5(12) + 6H = 180 \implies 60 + 6H = 180 \implies 6H = 120 \implies H = 20\]
Thus, \(\mathrm{C_{60}}\) contains \(20\) six-membered rings and \(12\) five-membered rings. As illustrated in the central pentagon surrounded by five hexagons in the diagram, a six-membered ring is fused with both six-membered and five-membered rings, whereas a five-membered ring can fuse only with six-membered rings.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Total vertices: \((12 \times 5 + 20 \times 6)/3 = 180/3 = 60\), matching \(\mathrm{C_{60}}\). Hence, \(\mathrm{C_{60}}\) has \(20\) six-membered rings and \(12\) five-membered rings, and a five-membered ring fuses only with six-membered rings.

answer.text: \(20\) six-membered rings and \(12\) five-membered rings; a five-membered ring can fuse only with six-membered rings.
\(12\) six-membered rings and \(20\) five-membered rings; a five-membered ring can fuse with both five- and six-membered rings.
\(20\) six-membered rings and \(12\) five-membered rings; a five-membered ring can fuse with both five- and six-membered rings.
\(16\) six-membered rings and \(14\) five-membered rings; a six-membered ring can fuse only with five-membered rings.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_DIAGRAM_Q10 - Corner sharing and ring size in silica network

questiontext.text:
The diagrams below show (I) the basic tetrahedral \(\mathrm{SiO_4^{4-}}\) silicate unit and (II) a schematic of the three-dimensional covalent network of silicon dioxide (\(\mathrm{SiO_2}\)):

In the \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) crystal network, how many oxygen corners of each \(\mathrm{SiO_4}\) tetrahedron are shared with adjacent tetrahedra, and what ring size is formed by the alternating \(\mathrm{Si}\) and \(\mathrm{O}\) atoms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Diagram (I) depicts a discrete tetrahedral \(\mathrm{SiO_4^{4-}}\) unit with one \(\mathrm{Si}\) atom bonded to four \(\mathrm{O}\) atoms. Diagram (II) depicts the extended \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) network in which each \(\mathrm{Si}\) is bonded to four \(\mathrm{O}\) atoms and each \(\mathrm{O}\) bridges two \(\mathrm{Si}\) atoms.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
When an oxygen corner is shared between two \(\mathrm{SiO_4}\) tetrahedra, each shared oxygen contributes \(\frac{1}{2}\) oxygen atom to each silicon centre.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
If \(n\) out of \(4\) oxygen corners of each \(\mathrm{SiO_4}\) tetrahedron are shared between two tetrahedra, the \(\mathrm{O:Si}\) ratio is \((4 - n) + \frac{n}{2} = 4 - \frac{n}{2}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\), the \(\mathrm{O:Si}\) ratio is \(2\), so \(4 - \frac{n}{2} = 2 \implies n = 4\). Thus, all \(4\) oxygen corners of each \(\mathrm{SiO_4}\) tetrahedron are shared with adjacent tetrahedra to form a three-dimensional network. Counting the atoms around any closed loop in Diagram (II) gives \(4\) \(\mathrm{Si}\) atoms alternating with \(4\) \(\mathrm{O}\) atoms: \(\mathrm{Si-O-Si-O-Si-O-Si-O}\), which is an \(8\)-membered ring.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Sharing all \(4\) corners yields the neutral formula \(\mathrm{SiO_{4/2}} = \mathrm{SiO_2}\) and forms \(8\)-membered rings of alternating silicon and oxygen atoms.

answer.text: \(2\) oxygen corners are shared, forming \(6\)-membered rings.
All \(4\) oxygen corners are shared, forming \(8\)-membered rings.
\(3\) oxygen corners are shared, forming \(8\)-membered rings.
All \(4\) oxygen corners are shared, forming \(4\)-membered rings.
